detest.e: PIE word *tréyes From Middle French detester (French détester), from Latin dētestor (“to imprecate evil while calling the gods to witness", "denounce", "hate intensely”), from dē- + testor (“to testify, bear witness”), from testis (“a witness”); see test, testify. Doublet of detestate.

d.g: To thaw; unthaw; unfreeze.
d.x:
"That's like your saying dethawed when you mean defrosted."
He made only the slightest little grunt.

dethaw.e: From de- + thaw, by confusion with defrost or perhaps with words with null de- like defraud, decomplex.

d.g: To depose; to forcibly relieve a monarch of the monarchy.
d.x: And if it is a despot you would dethrone, see first that his throne erected within you is destroyed.

d.g: To remove any governing authority from power.
To remove from any position of high status or power.
d.x: “[…] I’m a dethroned elder child, remember. My temper isn’t so damned long as you sometimes think!”

d.g: To remove (something) from a position of power or paramount importance.
d.x:
All that was Good and Holy, is dethron’d,
And Lust, and Rapine are for justice own’d.

dethrone.e: Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- English throne English dethrone From de- + throne.

d.g: to remove ticks (parasitic arachnids) from
To explode, blow up
To combust or decompose supersonically via shock compression.
To cause to explode.
d.x: The engineers detonated the dynamite and watched the old building collapse.

d.g: To express sudden anger.

detonate.e: First attested in 1729; either borrowed from French détoner or directly from Latin dētonātus, perfect passive participle of dētonō (“to thunder down (strongly); (figuratively, of a person) to thunder, speak threateningly, to rage; to stop thundering”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from dē- (“off, from”) + tonō (“to …

d.g: To remove poison (or its effects) from.
To counteract, or make less poisonous.
To remove foreign and harmful substances from something.
To make something that is harmful more benign.
d.x: We can either break as a nation or find a way to detoxify our politics.

detoxify.e: Attested since 1905 (twelve years earlier than toxify), from de- + tox- + -ify. (Detoxicate is attested one year earlier, since 1904.)

d.g: To take away; to withdraw or remove.
To take credit or reputation from; to derogate; to defame or decry.
d.x: That calumnious critic […] / Detracting what laboriously we do.

detract.e: Borrowed from Middle French détracter, from Latin detractum, past participle of detraho.

d.g: To exit from a train; to disembark.
d.x: If you plan to detrain at the next stop, please begin gathering your belongings.

d.g: To remove (a passenger or passengers) from a train; to evacuate (passengers) from a train.
d.x: Following the accident passengers were detrained through the rear cab.

d.g: To reduce one's training, particularly during the offseason, in preparation for a cycle of retraining.
To transfer air from an organized air current to the surrounding atmosphere.
intransitivize
intransitivize
Alternative form of detribalize.
To cause (the members of a tribe) to lose their tribal culture.
To remove the tusks from (an elephant, a boar, etc.).
To devalue, reduce in value.
To lower or remove the value of something.
To lose value; to depreciate.

devalue.e: Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- English value English devalue From de- + value.

d.g: To ruin many or all things over a large area, such as most or all buildings of a city, or cities of a region, or trees of a forest.
d.x: Halifax in Canada was devastated by a ship exploding in 1917. SS Mont Blanc, a French vessel loaded with 2.9 kilotons of explosives, collided with the Imo.

d.g: To destroy a whole collection of related ideas, beliefs, and strongly held opinions.
To break beyond recovery or repair so that the only options are abandonment or the clearing away of useless remains (if any) and starting over.
To greatly demoralize, to cause to suffer intense grief or dismay

devastate.e: Borrowed from Latin dēvastātus, perfect passive participle of dēvastō (“to lay waste, devastate”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)); from dē- (augmentative prefix) + vastō (“to destroy, lay waste”). See vast. First attested in 1638.

d.g: To remove the vein-like colon from (shrimp).

devein.e: Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- English vein English devein From de- + vein.

d.g: To change with a specific direction, progress.
d.x: Let's see how things develop and then make our decision.

d.g: To progress through a sequence of stages.
d.x: Isabel developed from a tropical depression to a tropical storm to a hurricane. An embryo develops into a fetus and then into an infant.

d.g: To advance; to further; to promote the growth of.
d.x: We must develop our own resources to the utmost.

d.g: To create.
d.x: I need to develop a plan for the next three weeks.

develop.e: Borrowed from French développer, from Middle French desveloper, from Old French desveloper, from des- + voloper, veloper, vloper (“to wrap, wrap up”) (compare Italian sviluppare, Old Italian alternative form goluppare (“to wrap”)) from Vulgar Latin *vloppō, *wloppō (“to wrap”) ultimately from Proto-Germanic *wrappaną, …

d.g: turn into a devil or make devilish
To represent as a devil.
d.x: He that should deify a saint, should wrong him as much as he that should devilize him.

devilize.e: Ancient Greek διαβάλλω (diabállō) Ancient Greek διάβολος (diábolos)bor. Latin diabolusbor. Proto-West Germanic *diubul Old English dēofol Middle English devel English devil Proto-Indo-European *-id- Proto-Indo-European *-yéti Proto-Indo-European *-idyéti Proto-Hellenic *-íďďō Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. …

d.g: Alternative form of devitalize.
To deprive of vitality; to make lifeless; to weaken.
d.x: Near-synonym: deanimate

devitalize.e: Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- English vitalize English devitalize From de- + vitalize.

d.g: To become crystalline and brittle
To pronounce a sound with little or no vibration of the vocal cords, especially a sound that is normally pronounced with such vibration (i.e. a voiced sound).
d.x: Lastly, as shown in the consonant table above, h- causes any following consonant to be devoiced[.]

d.g: To remove the voice flag from a user on IRC, preventing them from sending messages to the channel.

devoice.e: Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē-der. English de- Proto-Indo-European *wekʷ-der. Proto-Indo-European *wṓkʷs Proto-Italic *wōks Latin vōcem Anglo-Norman voizbor. Middle English voys English voice English devoice From de- + voice.

d.g: To be inherited by someone else; to pass down upon the next person in a succession, especially through failure or loss of an earlier holder.
To delegate (a responsibility, duty, etc.) on or upon someone.
d.x: Near-synonyms: pass down, pass on, hand down

d.g: To transfer authority and responsibility for (something) to (another entity).
d.x: Despite being a unitary state, the Government of the United Kingdom devolved many matters to the Governments of Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

d.g: To fall as a duty or responsibility on or upon someone.

devolve.e: Proto-Indo-European *de Proto-Indo-European *-h₁ Proto-Indo-European *déh₁ Proto-Italic *dē Latin dē Latin dē- Proto-Indo-European *welH-der. Proto-Italic *wolwō Latin volvō Latin dēvolvōbor. English devolve Borrowed from Latin dēvolvō (“roll or tumble off or down”), from dē- + volvō (“roll”).

d.g: to give one's time, focus one's efforts, commit oneself, etc. entirely for, on, or to a certain matter; to consecrate.
d.x: They devoted their lives to following Jesus Christ.

d.g: to consign over; to doom
d.x: to devote one to destruction

d.g: to execrate; to curse

devote.e: Borrowed from Latin dēvōtus, past participle of Latin dēvoveō (“dedicate by a vow, sacrifice oneself, promise solemnly”). Doublet of devow; see also devout. Displaced native Middle English ēstful, from Old English ēstful.

d.g: To eat quickly, greedily, hungrily, or ravenously.
d.x: Once constituted, capital reproduces itself faster than output increases. The past devours the future.

d.g: To rapidly destroy, engulf, or lay waste.
d.x: The fire was devouring the building.

d.g: To take in avidly with the intellect or with one's gaze.
d.x: She intended to devour the book.

d.g: To absorb or engross the mind fully, especially in a destructive manner.
d.x: After the death of his wife, he was devoured by grief.

devour.e: Inherited from Middle English devouren, from Old French devorer (Modern French dévorer), from Latin dēvorō, from vorō.

d.g: Described or set down in writing; portrayed. (archaic)
